title: Caol mhòr's settlers set aside the marked midden stones
summary: Households raising walls from the Old Ones' shell midden at Caol mhòr will not turn a stone that carries a mark, cut or worn, and lay those aside in an unmortared line along the shore, so that two kinds of wall stand side by side there ever after.

title: Somhairle walks the ground at Baile chrom
summary: Somhairle finds the resettled fields at Baile chrom already byred and welled, and Donnchadh Ruadh shows him the old field-marks still standing half sunk beneath the new grass, ploughed by hands no household there now names aloud.

title: The last thicket on the salt road is cut through
summary: Carriers weary of the long way round cut through the last unbroken stand of thorn and birch on the salt road to the north-west, so that Muileann àrsaidh stands a full day nearer the pans of Baile ghorm than it had ever stood before.

title: The first bank is turned east of the old workings
summary: Settlers pushing toward the rising country dig a ditch and raise the spoil behind it at Dùn thais, a ring of earth built without any word sent from Dùn ìseal and without any word sent back once it stood.

title: Fire clears the heavy ground at Achadh chaol
summary: Across three dry summers the households of Achadh chaol burn back the old scrub a field's width at a time and plough the black ground while the ash still holds its warmth, taking the first year a crop the older fields to the west had not equalled in a generation.

title: The last course is set on Cuan ruadh's wall
summary: The households of Cuan ruadh finish laying stone to the eaves the whole circuit of the settlement, the first roofs on that coast built to stand against wind rather than merely to be raised again once it has passed.

title: A well is opened within Cathair fhada's bank
summary: Cathair fhada digs and lines a well inside its own earthwork, so that a household need not send its water-carriers down to the shore while a storm still has teeth in it.

title: Caol ruadh's fishers mark the strait's channels
summary: The fishers of the narrow strait take to tying woven buoys over the deep channels where the current runs hardest, a small custom that spreads along the coast in a carrier's mouth the way the paired tide-marks spread before it.

title: Households come down to Doire ghlas
summary: Families out of the near valleys settle in the grove where the king kept his seven nights, drawn by its shelter and its old cleared paths, and mark timber in the oaks themselves for the first of their new byres.

title: Somhairle asks the household to spare three oaks
summary: Finding the three oldest trunks of the grove marked for the axe, Somhairle asks Fearchar mac Ailig's household to take their roof-beams elsewhere, giving no reason beyond that his father once set six pots beneath those particular trees.

title: The three oaks are spared
summary: The household cuts its beams instead from younger growth a short walk east and leaves the three old trunks standing at the centre of the new settlement, ringed within a generation by houses that call the place only the ring under the oaks.

title: Somhairle finds grey in his beard
summary: A cheese-seller on the road through the near valleys remarks on the grey coming into Somhairle's beard, and he finds at a still pool that she has told him true: the first lines his face has shown in two thousand four hundred and thirty-five years.

title: Beathan sees his father's face has changed
summary: Coming on Somhairle unexpectedly at the slab, Beathan stops in the doorway before he crosses it, having seen in his father's face the beginning of an ageing neither of them has yet spoken of aloud.
